title: Weak verbs

objectives.can: Parse forms of verbs with a weak first, middle or last root consonant and restore the root.

explanation.summary: Most Aramaic verbs have three firm root consonants, and the stems you have learned add prefixes, endings and vowels around them. A weak verb has a root consonant that does not hold firm: it assimilates, turns into a vowel, or disappears. Some of the commonest verbs are weak, so reading Daniel and Ezra means being able to restore the root behind a short, odd-looking form.

sections.heading: What 'weak' means, and how to restore a root
body: A root consonant is weak when it is one of נ, י, ו, א, ה, or when the second and third consonants are the same letter. The weakness shows in one of a few ways: the consonant is swallowed by the one after it (assimilation), it becomes a vowel, or it drops out.

Weak verbs are named for the place of the weak consonant. First-nun verbs have נ as the first consonant (נְפַל 'fall'). First-yod verbs have י (יְדַע 'know'). First-aleph verbs have א (אֲמַר 'say'). Hollow verbs have a vowel letter in the middle (קוּם 'arise'). Final-weak verbs end in a vowel letter, ה or א (בְּנָא 'build', עֲנָה 'answer'). Geminate verbs have a doubled last consonant (עֲלַל 'go in').

To restore a root, first strip what is not root: the prefixes (וְ-, לְ-, the person letters of the imperfect, the stem's own prefix) and the endings. Then count what is left. Three firm consonants, and you are done. Fewer than three, or a long vowel where a consonant should be, means a weak verb. A final vowel points to a final-weak verb; a long vowel between two consonants to a hollow or a geminate verb; a doubled first consonant after a prefix to an assimilated נ; an א right after the person letter to a first-aleph verb. The headword the corpus gives is the safe answer: it lists the root in its full form.

The three paradigm tables of this lesson show only forms that occur as bare words, and each has gaps. For הָוָא the perfect has the third person (singular and plural), the first and second singular, but no first or second plural. For קוּם the imperfect has only the third person in the Peal. For אֲמַר the imperfect has the third masculine singular, the first plural and the second plural, and no other person. A dash always means that the form does not occur in the texts, not that it cannot exist.

sections.heading: Final-weak verbs
body: These are the biggest class: הָוָא 'be', בְּנָא 'build', חֲזָא 'see', בְּעָא 'ask', רְמָה 'cast', שְׁנָא 'change', עֲנָה 'answer', מְטָא 'reach' and קְרָא 'call, read'. The corpus files them under a headword that ends in ה or א; the two letters are alternate spellings of the same final vowel, and the headword is not always the same letter as the one in the form you meet.

In the Peal perfect the third masculine singular ends in a vowel letter: חֲזָה, מְטָה, בְּעָא, הֲוָה. The feminine adds -ת straight after the vowel: עֲנָת, מְטָת, הֲוָת. The third masculine plural has no root consonant at all after the middle one, only the ending -וֹ: עֲנוֹ, רְמוֹ, מְטוֹ, שְׁנוֹ. When the ending begins with a consonant the weak consonant shows as י: חֲזֵית 'I saw', חֲזַיְתָ 'you saw', רְמֵינָא 'we cast'. The Peil (A3.1.1) has -יו in the plural: רְמִיו.

In the imperfect the last vowel is -ֵא or -ֵה: יִבְעֵה 'he will ask', תִשְׁנֵא 'it will change', אֶקְרֵא 'I shall read'. The plural ends in -וֹן: יִבְנוֹן 'they will build', יִקְרוֹן 'they will read'.

The participle of the masculine singular ends in -ֵה or -ֵא: חָזֵה, עָנֵה, בָּעֵא, קָרֵא. The masculine plural ends in -ַיִן: חָזַיִן, עָנַיִן, בָעַיִן, בָּנַיִן. The feminine ends in -ְיָה (singular) or -ְיָן (plural): שָׁנְיָה, שָׁנְיָן. The infinitive of the Peal begins with מִ-: לְמִבְנֵא 'to build', לְמִרְמֵא 'to cast', לְמִקְרֵא 'to read', לְמִבְעֵא 'to ask'.

The verb 'be' (הָוָא) is final-weak, but it keeps its middle consonant ו as a consonant before endings: הֲווֹ 'they were', and the imperfect begins with a ל in place of the י of the third masculine, לֶהֱוֵא. It is treated in A3.1.3.

sections.heading: Hollow verbs
body: A hollow verb has a vowel letter (ו or י) in the middle of the root. The headwords קוּם 'arise', שׂוּם 'set', תּוּב 'return' and דּוּר 'dwell' are written with the vowel ו in the middle. The perfect of the Peal drops it and has a long vowel: קָם 'he arose' is in the corpus only with a prefix (וְקָם), but its plural is קָמוּ; שָׂם, שָׂמוּ, שָׂמְתָּ 'you set'.

The imperfect keeps the vowel ו: יְקוּם 'he will arise', תְּקוּם 'she will arise', יְקוּמוּן 'they will arise', יְתוּב 'he will return', תְּדוּר 'it will dwell'. The imperative also keeps it: קוּמִי 'arise' (feminine) and שִׂימוּ 'set' (plural).
The participle puts a glide where the vowel was: the א of קָאֵם and קָאֲמַיָּא, the י of וְקָיְמִין and דָיְרִין. The Haphel has י: הֲקֵים 'he set up', הֲתִיב 'he returned'.
The corpus tags שִׂים as a Peil in some places and a Peal in others; the hollow root makes the two forms of the perfect look alike. Read the sense.

sections.heading: First-nun, first-yod and first-aleph verbs
body: A first-nun verb loses its נ in the imperfect when the next consonant has no vowel: the נ is replaced by doubling the next consonant. The imperfect of נְפַל 'fall' is יִפֵּל, not a form with נ; the plural is תִּפְּלוּן. The נ is kept in the perfect (נְפַל) and the participle (נָפְלִין), and it is lost in the imperative: פֻּקוּ 'go out!' from נְפַק. A verb need not follow the rule: נְתַן 'give' keeps its נ in יִנְתֵּן and תִּנְתֵּן, and loses it only when a suffix follows, in יִתְּנִנַּהּ 'he will give it'. In the Haphel the נ is back again: הַנְפֵּק 'he took out'.

A first-yod verb keeps its י in the perfect (יְדַע 'he knew', יְדַעְתָּ 'you knew') and the participle (יָדַע, יָדְעִין). In the Peal imperfect a נ takes its place: תִנְדַּע 'you will know', וְאִנְדַּע 'and I shall know', יִנְדְּעוּן 'they will know'. The imperative is short: דַּע 'know!'. In the Haphel the י becomes וֹ: הוֹדַע 'he made known'. The verb 'give' (יְהַב, with its partner נְתַן) and 'be able' (יְכֵל: יוּכַל 'he will be able', יָכְלִין 'being able') are of this class, and are taken up again in A3.1.3.

A first-aleph verb has א as its first consonant. After the person letter of the imperfect the א carries a long vowel: יֵאמַר 'he will say', תֵּאמְרוּן 'you will say', נֵאמַר 'we shall say', יֵאכֻל 'he will eat'. The perfect has the vowel on the א as usual: אֲמַר, אֲכַלוּ, אֲזַל. The imperative may have a long or short vowel: אֱמַר 'say!', אֱמַרוּ 'say!' (plural), אֲכֻלִי 'eat!' (feminine), אֵזֶל 'go!'. The infinitive of אֲמַר is written two ways: לְמֵאמַר, where the א is written, and לְמֵמַר, where it is silent and not written.

sections.heading: Geminate verbs
body: A geminate verb has the same letter as its second and third consonant. The headword writes both (עֲלַל 'go in', דְּקַק 'be shattered'), but in the short forms they run together. The Peal perfect of עֲלַל is עַל 'he went in', עַלַּת 'she went in', and the participle plural is עָלִּין. The perfect plural of דְּקַק is דָּקוּ 'they were shattered'.

The Haphel of a geminate verb shows the doubling in the stem. The Haphel of דְּקַק has הַדִּקוּ 'they crushed' and תַּדִּק 'it will crush'; the Haphel of עֲלַל is הַנְעֵל 'he brought in', with a נ added after the ה. The Hophal of עֲלַל is הֻעַל 'he was brought in' (A3.1.1).

misunderstandings: Do not assume that a short form has lost nothing. A two-consonant form like עַל, קָם or דַּע is a weak verb with a missing consonant, not a different word.

A נ that is missing from the imperfect has not been 'forgotten': a doubled first consonant after the prefix (יִפֵּל) is where it went. But not every first-nun verb does this: נְתַן keeps it in יִנְתֵּן.
The ending -ית of חֲזֵית is not a feminine ending. It is the first person ending, with the י that stands for the weak last consonant.
A headword ending in ה is not different from one ending in א. The corpus spells them in one way or the other (חֲזָא, עֲנָה), and the forms of the verb show the same endings.

deeper.heading: Why Aramaic verbs lose their weak letters
body: The weak consonants נ, י, ו, א, ה are the ones that the Semitic languages in general treat in special ways. The stems you met earlier were described for strong roots; a weak root follows the same pattern, but its weak consonant is changed by the sounds around it. A grammar usually gives one table for each class, and a learner who knows one clear example of each class can read most of the weak forms in the texts.

examples.analysis: Four weak verbs. וְקָם (4) is the Peal perfect of the hollow verb קוּם, third masculine singular: Nebuchadnezzar 'rose up'; the middle consonant has become the long vowel. עָנֵה (6) is the Peal participle of the final-weak עֲנָה, 'answering'. רְמֵינָא (12) is the Peal perfect, first person plural, of רְמָה 'cast': the weak last consonant shows as the י of the ending, 'we cast'. עָנַיִן (16) is the masculine plural of the same participle.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: He answered and said: 'Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace; he spoke and said: 'Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, ye servants of God Most High, come forth, and come hither.' Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, came forth out of the midst of the fire.
